topic: Bezold-Jarisch: brady + hypotension in beach chair after interscalene
scene: Beach-chair shoulder surgery under an interscalene block. Twenty minutes after sitting up, HR and BP suddenly drop.
question: Most likely cause?
why: Sitting up pools blood. An underfilled, hard-contracting ventricle can trigger a vagal reflex: sudden bradycardia and hypotension. Lower the head, give fluid, atropine or ephedrine, and epinephrine if severe.
pearl: Beach chair plus sudden brady and hypotension: think Bezold-Jarisch, treat fast.
caption:
Beach chair, interscalene block, then HR 38 and BP 68/40. What's happening? 🪑
Sitting up pools blood, and an underfilled heart can fire a vagal reflex.
Head down, fluid, atropine or ephedrine. Epinephrine if it's severe.

scene: Mid-case, peak pressure jumps from 22 to 40. Plateau stays at 18. Tidal volume is unchanged.
question: Where's the problem?
why: Peak minus plateau reflects airway resistance. A wide gap puts the problem in the tube or airways: kink, secretions, biting, bronchospasm. Pass a suction catheter and listen. If both rise, think compliance.
pearl: Wide peak-plateau gap means resistance. Both rising means compliance.
caption:
Peak 40, plateau 18. Is it the tube or the lungs? 🫁
The gap between peak and plateau tells you where to look.
Wide gap = resistance (tube, secretions, bronchospasm). Both up = compliance.

slides.title: LAST: from first sign to lipid
slides.sub: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity can follow any block. Know the plan.

bullets: It can start with cardiac collapse, no warning
Call for help and the LAST kit

slides.body: Give 20% lipid emulsion early, at the first sign of serious toxicity, following your LAST checklist.
slides.pearl: Know where the lipid kit lives before you block.

bullets: Start ACLS; it may take a long time
Avoid vasopressin, beta and calcium channel blockers

caption:
Your patient tastes metal right after the block. Do you know the next steps? ⚠️
Swipe: recognize LAST, stop injecting, oxygenate, lipid emulsion early.
If arrest: ACLS with smaller epinephrine doses, and keep going.

scene: End of case. Eyes open, 5-second head lift, strong grip. The quantitative TOF ratio reads 0.70.
question: Extubate now?
why: Head lift and grip can be present well below a TOF ratio of 0.9, while swallowing and airway protection are still weak. Reverse as appropriate and confirm 0.9 or higher before extubating.
pearl: Measure, don't guess: TOF ratio of 0.9 or higher before extubation.
caption:
Strong grip, 5-second head lift, TOF ratio 0.70. Would you pull the tube? 🤔
Clinical signs can look fine while the airway muscles are still weak.
A measured TOF ratio of 0.9 or higher is the target.

topic: Venous air embolism: recognition and management (carousel)

slides.title: Venous air embolism: spot it, stop it
slides.sub: Sitting craniotomy. ETCO2 suddenly drops. What now?

bullets: Precordial Doppler or TEE catch it first
Tell the surgeon: flood the field
Lower the site below the heart if you can
Aspirate air from a multi-orifice central line
Left side down, head down if feasible

slides.body: Any time the surgical site sits above the heart: sitting craniotomy, beach-chair shoulder, central line placement.
slides.pearl: Sudden ETCO2 drop plus hypotension: think air embolism.

slides.title: Flood. Oxygen. Aspirate.
slides.body: Know the sequence before your first neuro case.

caption:
Sitting craniotomy and the ETCO2 suddenly falls. Air embolism? 🧠
Swipe for the clues and the sequence: flood the field, 100% O2, stop nitrous, aspirate.
Any site above the heart is at risk.

scene: TURP under spinal, 70 minutes in. The patient becomes confused, restless and nauseated.
question: Most likely cause?
why: Absorbed hypotonic irrigant causes fluid overload and dilutional hyponatremia: hypertension, bradycardia, confusion, seizures. Ask the surgeon to finish, check sodium, treat overload, and correct severe hyponatremia carefully.
pearl: An awake patient under spinal is your best TURP syndrome monitor.
caption:
TURP under spinal: confused, BP 172/96, HR 48. What's going on? 🧪
Irrigant absorption: fluid overload plus dilutional hyponatremia.
That's why we like these patients awake: mental status is the monitor.
Comment A, B, C or D 👇

slides.title: 5 capnograms every student should know
slides.sub: Read the waveform, not just the number.

slides.body: Slow upstroke, no clean plateau. Think bronchospasm, COPD or a kinked tube.
A notch in the plateau: the patient is breathing against the ventilator. The block or anesthetic is wearing off.
No trace after intubation: esophageal until proven otherwise. Mid-case: disconnect, total obstruction or arrest.
A sudden drop with hypotension: low cardiac output or embolism (air, clot, CO2). Also check for a leak.
Rebreathing CO2. Check for exhausted absorbent or a stuck expiratory valve.
slides.pearl: Look at the shape every time you glance at the monitor.

slides.title: Read the shape.
slides.body: Save this for your next case.

caption:
Can you name these 5 capnogram shapes? 📈
Shark fin, curare cleft, flat line, sudden fall, rising baseline.
Each one points you to a different problem.
